candidates.title: Do not assume LLMs resist injected context; treat coherent tool output as able to override parametric memory
candidates.rule: When a tool or retriever supplies a single coherent passage, assume the model will adopt it over its own knowledge; gate third-party tool output through validation before it reaches the model instead of relying on model skepticism.
candidates.passage: LLMs are actually highly receptive to external evidence if it is presented in a coherent way , even though it conflicts with their parametric memory.
candidates.finding: Entity-substitution counter-evidence (word-level edits) was largely ignored, reproducing prior work, but LLM-generated coherent counter-evidence was adopted in most cases as the sole evidence, including fabricated/disinformation passages. Manual check of 50 stubborn cases attributed most to commonsense or weak conflict.
candidates.conditions: Zero-shot multiple-choice QA with memory answer, counter-answer, and 'Uncertain' options; counter-memory generated by ChatGPT; examples filtered by NLI entailment and answer-consistency checks.
candidates.limitations: Multiple-choice format, not free-form agent tasks; filtered dataset biased toward firm parametric memory; 2023 model versions; no test of any defense mechanism, so the validation-gate recommendation is the authors' suggestion rather than a measured intervention.
candidates.validation_test: In your retrieval-augmented pipeline, inject a fluent but factually wrong passage for questions the model answers correctly closed-book, and measure how often the answer flips with and without a source-credibility filter.

candidates.title: Consolidate fragmented evidence and avoid bare-answer snippets for claims that contradict the model
candidates.rule: Before handing retrieved evidence to the model, merge fragments that jointly support one conclusion into a single passage, and give contradicting claims full explanatory text rather than a bare answer string; short or fragmented support loses to longer, intact passages.
candidates.passage: shorter counter-memory evidence (counter-answer) is less likely to be considered by LLMs (56.7% to 18.8%)
candidates.location: Appendix A.2, Additional Knowledge Conflict Discussion (Table A.1)
candidates.finding: With ChatGPT on PopQA, replacing counter-memory with the bare counter-answer dropped its selection from 56.7% to 18.8%, while shortening the memory-aligned evidence barely changed preference (42.7% to 43.9%). On StrategyQA, fragmenting one side's evidence shifted ChatGPT to the intact opposing evidence in 38.2% of examples.
candidates.conditions: Multi-source multiple-choice setting with one memory-aligned and one counter passage; fragmentation test used StrategyQA's per-sub-question human-written facts.
candidates.limitations: Only ChatGPT tested for the length and fragmentation analyses; length is used as a proxy for persuasiveness with no matched-content control, so longer text may simply confound with more detail; single dataset pair.
candidates.validation_test: Take queries where your retriever returns several short snippets supporting one answer and one long passage supporting another; compare answer accuracy when snippets are concatenated into one coherent passage versus listed separately.

reason: The paper runs controlled experiments across eight LLMs on PopQA and StrategyQA comparing evidence construction methods, evidence order, quantity and irrelevant-evidence conditions. Several results translate into scoped harness rules about how retrieved/tool evidence is assembled and presented, though all are single-paper, multiple-choice QA findings with 2023-era models.
